notes: Recruited by trustee and state senator Charles E. Bush, who was touring Southern agricultural schools for the new First District Agricultural School's board; Kays began June 1, 1910 and welcomed the first 189 students on October 3, 1910. His title evolved from principal to president as the school grew into a four-year college; he resigned in January 1943 after nearly 33 years, having led the institution through two world wars, the Depression and the 1931 fire that destroyed the main building.

A 1925 Aggie alumnus who succeeded V. C. Kays as the institution's second president in January 1943 and resigned in June 1945. His next role is not immediate: University of Arkansas at Monticello's official history records him as being named president of Arkansas A&M College in 1949, four years after he left Jonesboro. What he did between 1945 and 1949, and what he did immediately before 1943, could not be verified.

Second, interim stint. After Horace Thompson resigned in June 1945, Kays, who had stayed on campus as president emeritus and business manager, resumed the chief executive role for roughly a year until W. J. Edens arrived in April 1946. A wholly internal appointment. Kays died in 1966; the historic V. C. Kays House is an A-State heritage site.

Appointed Arkansas State's third president in April 1946, ending Kays's interim service. Edens resigned on March 21, 1951, after which Dean J. Walter Turner served as acting president. Neither his prior position nor his subsequent career could be verified from official or archival sources; the university's own history refers to him only as 'W. J. Edens.'

Internal caretaker appointment. The sitting dean of the college was named acting president on March 21, 1951, the day President Edens resigned, and served until the trustees named Carl R. Reng president on April 3, 1951, a vacancy filled in less than a month. What he did after the acting stint is not documented in the university's published history.

priorTitle: Head of the school administration division of the Graduate School
notes: External hire from the University of Arkansas, named fourth president on April 3, 1951, less than a month after Edens resigned. Over 24 years enrollment grew from 863 students and 81 faculty to more than 7,300 students and 342 faculty, and he led the successful campaign for university status in 1967, making Arkansas State the state's second university. Retired in 1975; the Reng Student Union is named for him. Died 1988.

External hire; a former Razorback football and track athlete and Peace Corps official who had managed an international company's interests in Iran before becoming president of Hood College in Maryland in 1972. Took office at Arkansas State in August 1975 and was credited with recruiting minority students and faculty, reorganizing the agriculture department and founding the Center for Continuing Education. Left in 1978 to become chancellor of the University of Denver, where he served until 1984. Died 2020.

External hire from the University of Arkansas, where he had been assistant to the president and vice president for governmental relations and public affairs before returning as vice president. At Arkansas State he created Convocation of Scholars Week and an agricultural cooperative program with the University of Arkansas. Resigned in January 1980 to enter private business, becoming president and CEO of the Arkansas electric cooperatives; a former legislator, he later served as a special assistant to President Bill Clinton. Died 2005.

First of Smith's two interim presidencies. A 1952 alumnus and long-time internal administrator, he was named interim president when Carl Whillock resigned in January 1980 and served until Ray Thornton took office later that year, then returned to his senior administrative post. Encyclopedia of Arkansas lists vice president for administration, dean of the Graduate School and senior vice president among his pre-presidential titles but does not date each transition, so his exact title at each moment is not fully documented.

priorInstitution: Joint Educational Consortium (Ouachita Baptist University and Henderson State University)
notes: Seventh president and an external hire. A former Arkansas attorney general and three-term U.S. Representative, he lost a 1978 Senate bid and returned to Arkansas in 1979 as executive director of the Joint Educational Consortium, the post he held immediately before Arkansas State. At ASU he raised the faculty's role in governance, reinstituted an interdisciplinary Honors Program and built an international training program for Saudi customs officers. In 1984 he was offered the University of Arkansas presidency without a formal search after the incumbent resigned unexpectedly; he later returned to Congress and served on the Arkansas Supreme Court. Died 2016.

Internal promotion, not an external hire: a 1952 ASC graduate who joined the faculty in 1958 and rose through executive assistant to President Reng, vice president for administration, dean of the Graduate School and senior vice president before being named the eighth president effective February 15, 1984, after Thornton left for the University of Arkansas. Enrollment grew from 8,319 in fall 1984 to 10,416 in fall 1991; he established the first doctoral program, opened the Convocation Center, expanded Dean B. Ellis Library and moved athletics to Division I. Announced retirement in August 1991 and was named president emeritus June 30, 1992. Died September 23, 2018.

Ninth president, hired in 1992 when Eugene Smith retired; implemented leadership and quality-assurance programs. His administration lasted only two years and he departed in spring 1994, triggering an unusually chaotic succession. Biographical directories report he came to Jonesboro from a provost and vice chancellor for academic affairs role at the University of New Orleans (1989-1992), after deanships at Texas Christian University, but this could not be confirmed against any official university, archival or news source, so the prior-role fields are left blank. His subsequent career is likewise unverified.

Internal appointment. The sitting vice president for academic affairs stepped up as interim president on Mangieri's departure in spring 1994 but died suddenly several months into the term, the first of two sudden deaths of long-time ASU administrators in the same year.

Internal appointment. Succeeded Hoskins as interim president in summer 1994 and died that fall, the second sudden death of a popular long-time university administrator within months. An Arkansas State student affairs award is named in his memory; he had also served as president of the Arkansas Student Affairs Association.

Third stint leading the campus and second interim presidency. Two years after retiring, the board called Smith back out of retirement to steady the university following the deaths of Hoskins and Richmond, and he ran the institution through the 1994-95 academic year while leading the nationwide search that produced Les Wyatt. Returned to retirement in summer 1995.

Tenth president, effective July 1, 1995, recruited from the University of Mississippi after the extensive national search run by interim president Eugene Smith; he had earlier held posts at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock from 1977 to 1988. Ushered in a new era of campus building expansion and served as both president of the emerging system and chief executive of the Jonesboro campus until the first Jonesboro chancellor was installed in fall 2006, when he moved to the system presidency full time. Resigned as system president in 2010 and was named president emeritus of the ASU System.

First chancellor of the Jonesboro campus and an external hire, appointed in the fall 2006 administrative reorganization that formally created the ASU System office and left Les Wyatt as system president. A lawyer by training (Alabama JD, Harvard LLM), he had been general counsel of the University of Alabama System, president of the University of North Alabama from 1990 to 2004, then chancellor of the North Dakota University System. Enrollment rose 23%, fundraising and research funding set records, and he created the Chancellor's Circle and the Beck Center for Veterans. In 2010 the trustees asked him to serve as interim system president; he retired in 2011 once Charles Welch was appointed and returned to Florence, Alabama. Died October 27, 2022.

priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Research and Provost
notes: Internal elevation: the sitting provost, who had come to A-State in 2007, was made interim chancellor in 2010 when Robert Potts moved to the interim system presidency, and led the campus for about two years. Known for a renewed push on international programs that sharply grew international enrollment and for launching online degree programs. Returned to full-time tenured faculty status in 2012 when Tim Hudson arrived, and was named chancellor of Louisiana State University of Alexandria in January 2014. An Army veteran with two doctorates, he died suddenly on January 30, 2022.

Second chancellor of the Jonesboro campus and an external hire: named March 2, 2012 and took office May 1, 2012, coming from a vice chancellor role at the Texas Tech University System that he had held since 2011, after serving as president of the University of Houston-Victoria (2004-2010) and provost at the University of Southern Mississippi. Resigned abruptly on August 3, 2016, effective immediately, after internal audits into nepotism and conflicts of interest in the study-abroad program his wife had overseen as part-time director. His subsequent role is not documented.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Research
notes: Internal stopgap. ASU System President Charles L. Welch named the sitting provost acting chancellor on August 3, 2016, the day Tim Hudson resigned, and she ran the campus for roughly a month until Doug Whitlock's interim appointment took effect in September 2016, after which she resumed the provost role. A 1979 A-State graduate who joined the biological sciences faculty in 1993 and had been dean of University College and associate dean of Arts and Sciences.

Brought out of retirement as a caretaker by ASU System President Charles L. Welch, starting September 12, 2016 on a prorated $305,000 salary through June 30, 2017, and expressly barred from candidacy for the permanent chancellorship so that a clean national search could begin in spring 2017. Then 73, he had spent 45 years at Eastern Kentucky University, including an interim presidency that became permanent, retiring as president in 2013.

priorTitle: Dean, College of Arts and Sciences
notes: Third chancellor and an external hire, announced May 17, 2017 and effective July 1, 2017, succeeding interim chancellor Doug Whitlock after a national search that drew 53 viable applications and brought three finalists to campus; the search advisory committee recommended him unanimously. He had been dean of the University of Oklahoma's College of Arts and Sciences since 2013. Announced on March 31, 2022 that he would resign effective June 30, 2022 to become president of Texas State University, where he started July 1, 2022.

priorTitle: Dean, J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences
notes: Fourth chancellor and an external hire from the University of Arkansas, where he had been Fulbright College dean since 2014; selected July 11, 2022 at a $450,000 salary and first day in office August 15, 2022. Because Damphousse left June 30 and Shields did not start until mid-August, the campus went roughly six weeks in summer 2022 with no publicly named interim chancellor. Enrollment grew nearly 30% under Shields and he launched the College of Veterinary Medicine, the Center for Advanced Materials and Steel Manufacturing and the CREST Center workforce program. On May 26, 2026 the ASU System Board of Trustees unanimously selected him as the system's fourth president, effective July 1, 2026, succeeding Brendan Kelly, who left in December 2025 to lead Eastern Michigan University; Robin Myers served as interim system president until Shields took over.

Internal appointment, not an external hire: interim system president Robin Myers recommended the sitting provost and executive vice chancellor, and the ASU System Board of Trustees voted unanimously on May 26, 2026 to name him interim chancellor effective July 1, 2026, the same day Shields became system president. He is the first African American to serve as either provost or chancellor at Arkansas State. A historian and native Arkansan with a Ph.D. from the University of Mississippi, he joined A-State as provost on July 1, 2023 from the University of Arkansas, where he had spent nearly 20 years and was associate dean of humanities in Fulbright College; as provost he took Arkansas's first and only College of Veterinary Medicine from concept to a first class in fall 2026 and oversaw growth past 17,000 students. As of July 24, 2026 neither A-State nor the ASU System had publicly announced a chancellor search committee, search firm or timeline for the Jonesboro campus; William McLean is serving as interim provost.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same institution, internal continuation; he had led ASU since July 1, 1995, before the 2006 system reorganization)
notes: First president of the ASU System. Formally titled James Leslie Wyatt, he became ASU president on July 1, 1995 and in October 2006 the Board of Trustees created a separate system office, with Wyatt remaining as system president and Robert L. Potts named the first chancellor of the Jonesboro campus. He announced his resignation at the May 2010 quarterly board meeting, effective June 30, 2010, and was unanimously designated President Emeritus.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal appointment)
notes: Asked by the Board of Trustees to serve as interim system president from July 1, 2010 while a permanent successor to Les Wyatt was recruited; Dan Howard became interim Jonesboro chancellor on his recommendation. Potts had been president of the University of North Alabama (1990-2004), general counsel of the University of Alabama System, and chancellor of the North Dakota University System before becoming ASU-Jonesboro's first chancellor in fall 2006. He retired to Florence, Alabama in 2011 and died October 28, 2022.

priorInstitution: Henderson State University, Arkadelphia, Arkansas (a separate Arkansas public university, not in the ASU System)
notes: Second president of the ASU System, known publicly as Chuck Welch. Named by the Board of Trustees in November 2010 and formally beginning in April 2011, he became the longest-tenured higher education president or chancellor in Arkansas over nearly 13 years. Earlier ASU System and Arkansas roles included chancellor of UA Community College at Hope-Texarkana and vice chancellor for academic affairs at ASU-Beebe. He resigned in November 2023, was designated President Emeritus in December 2023, and became AASCU's seventh president and CEO on January 15, 2024; the ASU System's own timeline lists his tenure as 2011-2023.

priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus (retired Chancellor of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home)
priorInstitution: Arkansas State University-Mountain Home (same system, internal appointment)
notes: First of two interim presidencies. Announced December 8, 2023 and effective January 15, 2024, he was chosen for his familiarity with the system and its leadership; the board stated he would not be a candidate for the permanent job. He had retired in July 2023 after 11 years as chancellor of ASU-Mountain Home and was designated Chancellor Emeritus on July 18, 2023. He served until Brendan Kelly took office on September 23, 2024.

priorInstitution: University of West Georgia, Carrollton, Georgia
notes: Third president of the ASU System, selected by the Board of Trustees on June 5, 2024 and beginning September 23, 2024. He came from the University of West Georgia presidency, which he had held since 2020, after earlier service as chancellor of USC Upstate, interim president of the University of South Carolina, and vice president for advancement at the University of West Florida. He announced his departure on December 10, 2025 to become president of his alma mater Eastern Michigan University, starting there April 1, 2026.

priorTitle: Chancellor Emeritus of Arkansas State University-Mountain Home and ASU System consultant; previously interim ASU System president in 2024
priorInstitution: Arkansas State University System (same system, internal appointment)
notes: Second interim presidency. The Board of Trustees named him interim system president on December 12, 2025, effective immediately, on contract terms consistent with his previous interim service and without scheduling a permanent search at that meeting. He served until Todd Shields took office July 1, 2026, and recommended A-State provost Calvin White Jr. as interim Jonesboro chancellor.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (same system, internal promotion; he was chancellor from August 15, 2022 to June 30, 2026)
notes: Fourth president of the ASU System, appointed by unanimous vote of the Board of Trustees at a special called meeting on May 26, 2026, effective July 1, 2026, succeeding Brendan Kelly (with Robin Myers serving as interim in between). A political scientist with a Ph.D. from the University of Kentucky, he was dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at the University of Arkansas from 2014 before being named A-State's chancellor on July 11, 2022, where he oversaw an enrollment increase of nearly 30 percent as the fourth appointed chancellor and 14th person to lead the Jonesboro campus.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College, which the Little Rock Board of Education created in 1927 and operated as a school-district institution. Hall held the college presidency while serving as Little Rock School District superintendent (1909-1941); Hall High School is named for him.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Larson, a Swedish-born high school principal, urged the Little Rock Board of Education to found LRJC in 1927 and is regarded as its founder; he resigned the Central High School principalship to devote himself to the college and died in office in 1949. The UA Little Rock official list gives 1930-1949; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas photo caption dates his presidency from 1929 and the UA Little Rock history page says 1930-1950.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Published as Granville D. Davis by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, which notes he was a member of the first LRJC graduating class, making him an alumnus-president. His immediately prior and subsequent positions could not be verified from available sources.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: acting president of Little Rock Junior College, as published on the university's official list of past presidents and chancellors. He bridged the two years between Granville Davis and Carey V. Stabler; no verifiable record of his prior or subsequent positions was found.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: President. Under Stabler, Little Rock Junior College became the independent, private, four-year Little Rock University in fall 1957, and course offerings grew from roughly 80 in 1956 to about 500 by 1967. He continued in office when the institution joined the University of Arkansas System in 1969, at which point his title changed from president to chancellor. His position immediately before 1956 could not be verified.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorInstitution: Little Rock University (the same institution, before its 1969 merger into the UA System)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. Same person as the preceding entry, listed separately by the university because the 1969 merger of Little Rock University into the University of Arkansas System converted the office from president to chancellor. He resigned in 1972; Stabler Hall is named for him. What he did after resigning could not be verified.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: acting chancellor. Fribourgh, a biologist, joined Little Rock Junior College in 1949 and spent 45 years at the institution through its Little Rock University and UALR eras, serving as chief academic officer from 1969 to 1984 and stepping up as acting chancellor after Stabler's resignation. Fribourgh Hall and the university's Fribourgh Award are named for him; he died March 6, 2014.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Ross accepted the UALR chancellorship in January 1973 as chancellor and professor of education and psychology, and is credited with establishing UALR's autonomy within the UA System, growing degree programs from 28 to 73 and enrollment from about 3,500 to 9,652. He left in summer 1982, was named president of Western Washington University in January 1983, and was killed in a plane crash in November 1987 along with two WWU vice presidents and the pilot. He was also a past president of ACPA.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: acting chancellor. Fribourgh's second stint as acting chancellor, bridging G. Robert Ross's summer 1982 departure and James H. Young's arrival later that year; the university lists both of his acting terms in a single line (1972-1973, 1982).

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. Young emphasized a traditional liberal arts direction, established campus-wide learning goals, and opened UALR's first residential dormitory. His position immediately before 1982 and his destination after leaving in 1992 could not be verified from available sources; the University of Arkansas holds biographical materials on him in its archives.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: interim chancellor. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas records that Anderson, then UALR's provost, served as interim chancellor in 1993 between James H. Young and Charles E. Hathaway; the university's own official list of past chancellors omits this interim term.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Hathaway had chaired the physics department at Kansas State University for 16 years, then was dean of the College of Sciences and Engineering at the University of Texas at San Antonio (1981-1986) and vice president for academic affairs at Wright State University (1986-1993). As chancellor he returned UALR to an urban/metropolitan mission and created the Cyber College in 1998. He stayed on as a UALR faculty member after 2002 and died August 5, 2025, at age 89.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. A thoroughly internal appointment: Anderson joined UALR in 1971 as an assistant professor of political science, became founding dean of the graduate school in 1977 and provost in 1984, held the provostship for nearly two decades, and was named chancellor in 2003 after an earlier interim term. He served 13 years as chancellor and 45 years at the institution, oversaw the Donaghey College of Engineering, the Jack Stephens Center and three residence halls, and retired effective June 30, 2016; the Anderson Institute on Race and Ethnicity was named for him that year.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Executive Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs and Provost
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: interim chancellor. Named interim chancellor on June 28, 2016 upon Joel Anderson's June 30 retirement, she led the campus from July 1 to August 30, 2016, working closely with UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt until Andrew Rogerson began September 1. She was published as Zulma Toro-Ramos when hired as UALR provost in 2012, and in October 2016 was selected as the thirteenth president of Central Connecticut State University, taking office January 3, 2017 as that university's first female and first Hispanic president. She is omitted from the university's official past-chancellors list.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
priorInstitution: Sonoma State University (California State University system)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire: UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt selected Rogerson in May 2016 after an eight-month national search that produced three finalists, and he took office September 1, 2016 as the university's tenth chancellor, with an investiture on May 11, 2017. A native of Scotland with a doctorate in protozoan ecology, he had previously held posts at Marshall University and Fresno State. Amid enrollment decline and budget cuts he announced on August 30, 2019 that he would step down effective September 1, 2019, saying it would be best for him to step aside.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
priorTitle: Interim Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
notes: Title in effect: Chancellor; sitting incumbent, so endYear is null. A fully internal appointment: Drale joined UALR in 2006 as associate dean of the College of Professional Studies after nearly 20 years at Missouri State University, became associate vice chancellor for academic affairs in 2011, and was serving as interim executive vice chancellor and provost from October 2018 when UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt named her acting chancellor on September 4-5, 2019 after Andrew Rogerson's forced resignation; the UA Board of Trustees unanimously made the appointment permanent on September 12, 2019. She holds BA, MA and PhD degrees from UC San Diego. She told the UA Board of Trustees in May 2026 (reported May 21-22, 2026) that she will retire effective June 30, 2027, at the end of the 2026-27 academic year, saying "It's just time for me" after about 40 years in higher education, and wanting to finish the university's centennial year and its $250 million Centennial Campaign. UA System President Jay B. Silveria announced the advisory chancellor search committee on July 16, 2026 (reported by the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette on July 23, 2026), chaired by UALR vice provost for research and graduate dean Brian Berry and including UA trustee Ashley Caldwell and Little Rock city director Dean Kumpuris; the committee will work with a search firm and the position is to be advertised beginning early in the fall 2026 semester, with Silveria aiming to identify a successor before Drale departs.

priorInstitution: Little Rock, Arkansas public schools (previously Mattoon, Illinois public schools)
notes: Hired as acting president of the newly opened Arkansas Industrial University because the trustees could not secure a permanent leader; he organized the institution, managed its business affairs, hired faculty and taught courses. The university awarded him an honorary Master of Arts degree in 1880.

priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: A Yale graduate (1853) and former Union Army captain who had been the university's treasurer since its 1871 founding; Old Main opened during his presidency. He left when appointed state adjutant general and ran unsuccessfully for governor in 1875.

priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Second, non-acting term leading the university, returning to the presidency from the normal department after Albert Bishop's departure. He later became superintendent of the Fort Smith school district (1884) and of Fayetteville public schools (1889).

West Point graduate (1842) and Confederate lieutenant general who had chaired mathematics at Washington College and Davidson College before running the North Carolina Military Institute. His administration raised academic standards and grew enrollment; he resigned in 1884 for health reasons.

Virginia-born former Confederate officer whose administration emphasized institutional regulation, holding forty-two faculty meetings before Christmas of his first college year. He resigned in 1887 in opposition to a General Assembly reorganization of the university.

priorTitle: Chair of Mathematics and Logic (then acting president)
priorInstitution: Arkansas Industrial University (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Promoted from the mathematics and logic chair (1885-1887) to acting president and then confirmed as the university's fifth president. Student attendance rose to roughly 700 during his tenure, which a faculty report called a period of progress unprecedented in the institution's history.

priorTitle: Superintendent of Public Instruction of Virginia (and ex officio member of the University of Virginia board)
notes: A former president of Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, he changed the institution's name from Arkansas Industrial University to University of Arkansas in 1899 and created independent departments of history, civil engineering and electrical engineering. He retired in 1902 for health reasons and returned to Virginia.

A Baptist minister and educator, he was the first University of Arkansas president born after the Civil War and the youngest person to hold the office. He secured funding for several campus buildings still in use, and later entered educational publishing in St. Louis.

priorTitle: President of the alumni association and member of the Board of Trustees (previously prosecuting attorney and circuit judge, 4th Judicial District of Arkansas)
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: A lawyer admitted to the Arkansas bar in 1883, he came to the presidency from the university's own alumni association leadership and board of trustees. He resigned at the end of the 1911-1912 school year and was elected to Congress two years later, serving seven terms.

priorTitle: Chair of History and Political Science
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Acting president who reorganized the teaching departments into three colleges (Agriculture, Arts and Sciences, and Engineering) and created a publicity committee that became the university relations office. Despite campus support, the Board of Trustees passed him over for the permanent post.

priorTitle: Chair of the Mathematics Department (and acting president)
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Longest-serving president in the institution's history; enrollment nearly quadrupled and major campus buildings were constructed during his 26 years. He died in office in a traffic accident near West Fork, Arkansas, on September 12, 1939, while returning from business in Little Rock.

priorInstitution: University of Arkansas School of Law (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Elevated from the law faculty (which he joined in 1936) to the presidency at age 34. His presidency was terminated by trustees newly appointed by Governor Homer Adkins, whom Fulbright's mother Roberta, editor of the Northwest Arkansas Times, had opposed; he went on to the U.S. House in 1942, the Senate in 1944, and a long chairmanship of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

priorTitle: Registrar and Director of General Extension
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: The first Arkansas-born president of the university, promoted after serving as registrar since 1916 and extension director since 1919. He mobilized the campus for World War II, saying the University of Arkansas enlisted for the duration when Pearl Harbor was bombed; he resigned in 1946, served into early 1947, and died in Fayetteville that December.

An economist recruited from Bennington College who oversaw the racial integration of the university, when Silas H. Hunt enrolled in the School of Law, along with creation of the Fine Arts Center and the Medical Center at Little Rock. He left in 1951 for the Rutgers presidency and later led the National Conference of Christians and Jews.

Held a Princeton doctorate and served in the Navy in World War II; at Arkansas he won North Central Association accreditation of doctoral programs, launched the university's first major research push and established a School of Nursing at Fayetteville and the Little Rock Medical Center. He resigned in 1959 for the North Carolina State chancellorship.

priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Acting president named when John Tyler Caldwell resigned, having joined the university in 1954 as an assistant to the president for public relations. When Mullins was appointed president in 1960 he became vice president for health sciences, later leaving in 1970 for the National Institutes of Health.

Came to the presidency after eleven years (1949-1960) as vice president of Auburn University. He retired in 1974; the university's main research library is named in his honor, and he received honorary degrees from Hendrix College (1965) and the University of Arkansas (1987).

An agricultural economist with two decades at North Carolina State before four years as chancellor of the University of Maryland. He built the administrative architecture of what became the University of Arkansas System, creating an executive cabinet and appointing chancellors at the regional campuses, and oversaw construction of Kimpel Hall and a new business building.

priorTitle: Vice President for the Division of Agriculture
priorInstitution: University of Arkansas (same institution, internal appointment)
notes: Promoted from within after joining the University of Arkansas in 1975 as vice president for agriculture. As president he created the chancellor's position at the Fayetteville campus, founded the University of Arkansas Press, and built the Center for Continuing Education; he left in 1984 to become president of his alma mater Auburn University, retiring there in 1992.

priorInstitution: Arkansas State University, Jonesboro (a different Arkansas public system, not the UA System)
notes: A former Arkansas attorney general and congressman from the 4th District who came to the UA System presidency directly from three years as president of Arkansas State University in Jonesboro; he moved the president's office to Little Rock. He returned to politics for three more congressional terms, was elected to the Arkansas Supreme Court in 1996 and retired in 2004.

priorTitle: President of Corpus Christi State University (Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi); earlier chancellor of the three-campus South Texas University System
priorInstitution: Corpus Christi State University / Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, Texas
notes: A UA-Fayetteville alumnus who returned to his alma mater in 1990 after roughly 22 years in Texas higher education, including about 13 years leading the Corpus Christi institution. Enrollment in the UA System grew from about 30,000 students on five campuses to nearly 70,000 across 17 campuses and units, with roughly $2 billion in construction and renovation.

priorTitle: Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs
notes: A chemist and former dean of the J. William Fulbright College of Arts and Sciences at UA-Fayetteville (2003) who returned from UT Arlington to begin as system president on November 1, 2011. He founded eVersity, the state's first fully online institution, in 2015, added UA-Pulaski Technical College and UA-Rich Mountain (2016) and East Arkansas Community College (2024), and announced his retirement on July 16, 2024, effective January 15, 2025.

priorTitle: Associate Vice President of Texas A&M University and Executive Director of the Bush School of Government & Public Service in Washington, D.C.
notes: Retired U.S. Air Force lieutenant general and former superintendent of the U.S. Air Force Academy, unanimously approved by the University of Arkansas Board of Trustees on November 18, 2024 and started January 15, 2025. The search that produced him was run for the UA Foundation Board by Greenwood Asher & Associates (Julie Holley and Marion Frenche), with trustee Scott Ford leading; seven candidates formally applied. He remains in office, so the Greenwood Asher engagement is closed and there is no active UA System presidential search.
